title: “The foundations also of the hills moved” (Psalm 18) — “the foundations of heaven moved” (2 Samuel 22)
summary: The same line of David’s song reads in the KJV of Psalm 18:7 “the foundations also of the hills moved and were shaken”, and in 2 Samuel 22:8 “the foundations of heaven moved and shook”. Hills and heaven are different things.
text: KJV Psalm 18:7: “Then the earth shook and trembled; the foundations also of the hills moved and were shaken, because he was wroth.” KJV 2 Samuel 22:8: “Then the earth shook and trembled; the foundations of heaven moved and shook, because he was wroth.” Hebrew (WLC) Psalm 18:8 (the Hebrew count includes the title as verse 1): וַתִּגְעַ֬שׁ וַתִּרְעַ֨שׁ ׀ הָאָ֗רֶץ וּמֹוסְדֵ֣י הָרִ֣ים יִרְגָּ֑זוּ וַ֝יִּתְגָּֽעֲשׁ֗וּ כִּי־חָ֥רָה לֹֽו׃ Hebrew (WLC) 2 Samuel 22:8: [וַתְגָּעַשׁ כ] (וַיִּתְגָּעַ֤שׁ  ק) וַתִּרְעַשׁ֙ הָאָ֔רֶץ מֹוסְדֹ֥ות הַשָּׁמַ֖יִם יִרְגָּ֑זוּ וַיִּֽתְגָּעֲשׁ֖וּ כִּֽי־חָ֥רָה לֹֽו׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Psalm 17:8: Καὶ ἐσαλεύθη, καὶ ἔντρόμος ἐγενήθη ἡ γῆ, καὶ τὰ θεμέλια τῶν ὀρέων ἐταράχθησαν, καὶ ἐσαλεύθησαν, ὅτι ὠργίσθη αὐτοῖς ὁ Θεός. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Samuel 22:8: Καὶ ἐταράχθη καὶ ἐσείσθη ἡ γῆ, καὶ τὰ θεμέλια τοῦ οὐρανοῦ συνεταράχθησαν καὶ ἐσπαράχθησαν, ὃτι ἐθυμώθη Κύριος αὐτοῖς. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/18/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/22/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA017.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA22.htm.
reasoning: The two songs run in step: the earth shook and trembled, the foundations moved, because he was wroth. The word that follows “the foundations” differs. Psalm 18 has הָרִ֣ים (mountains or hills), and 2 Samuel 22 has הַשָּׁמַ֖יִם (the heavens). The Greek agrees with each Hebrew in its own place: τῶν ὀρέων (of the mountains) in Psalm 17:8 and τοῦ οὐρανοῦ (of the heaven) in 2 Samuel 22:8. A reader of the two books is told that what shook was the foundations of the hills in one and of heaven in the other.

It does not say that either book is wrong, that David sang both forms, or which wording is original; the KJV and the Hebrew and Greek texts all agree with each other in each place, so no tag applies. Both are poetry, and “foundations of heaven” and “foundations of the hills” may be two images for the same shaking of the world. The record states only that the words differ. title: “He did fly upon the wings of the wind” (Psalm 18) — “he was seen upon the wings of the wind” (2 Samuel 22)

title: “He will be our guide even unto death” — the Greek has “for the ages”
summary: The KJV ends the psalm “he will be our guide even unto death”. The Septuagint, in Brenton’s Greek, ends with αὐτὸς ποιμανεῖ ἡμᾶς εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας, “he will shepherd us to the ages”.
text: KJV Psalm 48:14: “For this God is our God for ever and ever: he will be our guide even unto death.” Hebrew (WLC) Psalm 48:15: כִּ֤י זֶ֨ה ׀ אֱלֹהִ֣ים אֱ֭לֹהֵינוּ עֹולָ֣ם וָעֶ֑ד ה֖וּא יְנַהֲגֵ֣נוּ עַל־מֽוּת׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Psalm 47:15: Ὅτι οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα καὶ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τοῦ αἰῶνος, αὐτὸς ποιμανεῖ ἡμᾶς εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας. [For this is our God to the age and to the age of the age; he will shepherd us to the ages.] Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/48/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA047.htm.
reasoning: The KJV sets an end point, death, to the guiding. The Greek has εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας (to the ages), which has no end point. The Hebrew closes with עַל־מֽוּת, and the KJV reading follows it. A reader of the English is told God guides his people until they die; a reader of the Greek is told he will shepherd them without end.
scope: T applies at 48:14 and only to the closing phrase; the verse’s first half (this God is our God for ever and ever) agrees. The difference found is between the KJV and the Greek. The Hebrew is quoted so that the three texts stand together; this record does not say what the Hebrew phrase means, whether it is a musical note or a time, or that “unto death” is wrong. This compares the wording of three texts and does not show which is original. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton's printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher's plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

title: “That seek thy face, O Jacob” — the Greek has “the face of the God of Jacob”
summary: In the KJV the seekers are addressed as “Jacob”, and the face they seek is “thy face”. The Septuagint, in Brenton’s Greek, has them seek τὸ πρόσωπον τοῦ Θεοῦ Ἰακώβ, “the face of the God of Jacob”.
text: KJV Psalm 24:6: “This is the generation of them that seek him, that seek thy face, O Jacob. Selah.” Hebrew (WLC) Psalm 24:6: זֶ֭ה דֹּ֣ור [דֹּרְשֹׁו כ] (דֹּרְשָׁ֑יו ק) מְבַקְשֵׁ֨י פָנֶ֖יךָ יַעֲקֹ֣ב סֶֽלָה׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Psalm 23:6: Αὕτη ἡ γενεὰ ζητούντων αὐτὸν, ζητούντων τὸ πρόσωπον τοῦ Θεοῦ Ἰακώβ. διάψαλμα. [This is the generation of those who seek him, who seek the face of the God of Jacob.] Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/24/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA023.htm.
reasoning: In the KJV the verse turns to speak to a person or a people named Jacob (“O Jacob”), and the face sought is the face of the one addressed earlier. In the Greek there is no address: the seekers seek τοῦ Θεοῦ Ἰακώβ, the God of Jacob. The Hebrew ends יַעֲקֹ֣ב, with the name and no word for God, and the KJV reading follows it. The English and the Greek therefore differ on whom the seekers seek and whether Jacob is spoken to.
scope: T applies at 24:6 and only to the last phrase; both texts agree that this is the generation of those who seek him. The WLC text also marks a written and a read form in the first half of the verse (דֹּרְשֹׁו and דֹּרְשָׁיו); that is not tagged here. The difference found is between the KJV and the Greek. The Hebrew is quoted so that the three texts stand together; this record does not say that “O Jacob” is the better reading or that the Greek adds a word.
